passages.t: Shiloh: ‘How long will you put off entering and possessing the land’
passages.happening:
“Then the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the Tent of Meeting there” (verse 1). The land lay subdued before them. But seven tribes still had no share.

Joshua puts a hard question to them. “How long will you put off entering and possessing the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?” (verse 3).

Then he gives a plan. Each of the seven tribes is to appoint three men. They are to walk the land that is left, describe it in writing, and divide it into seven portions. Judah will keep its place in the south and the house of Joseph in the north. When the description is brought back, ‘I will cast lots for you here in the presence of the LORD our God’ (verse 6).

The men go through the land ‘city by city’, write it up in seven parts, and bring the document to Joshua at Shiloh (verse 9). There he casts lots before the LORD and gives each tribe its portion (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The Tent of Meeting was the tabernacle, the tent of God's presence that Israel had carried through the wilderness. Until now it had moved with the camp. At Shiloh it is set up in a settled place in the middle of the land. Shiloh lay in the hills of Ephraim, and it stayed Israel's place of worship all through the time of the judges. Hannah prayed there for a child, and the boy Samuel grew up there.

So the rest of the land is divided with God's dwelling at the center and the tribes gathered around it. The first chapters of the book had the ark going ahead of a people on the march. Now the people are home, and God has made his home among them.

Joshua's question shows a new kind of problem. Two great tribes have their land. Seven have none, and they are in no hurry. They have peace, the camp is comfortable, and going out to settle a hillside is hard work. The Hebrew word behind ‘put off’ means to go slack. It does not describe rebellion. It describes a slow loss of will. The land has been given. It is simply not being taken up.

Joshua's cure for it is practical. He does not preach at length. He sends men out to look. The survey is one of the few places in the Old Testament where land is mapped for sharing out, and the men bring back a written record. Lists of this kind were common in the ancient world. A written description meant that the division was public and could be checked.

The lots are cast ‘in the presence of the LORD’, at the tent, with the priest there. That made the division an act of worship and a decision no tribe could later dispute.

Verse 7 says again that the Levites get no portion of land, and gives the reason in a fresh form: ‘their inheritance is the priesthood of the LORD’.
passages.later:
Shiloh's later story is a warning. When Israel treated the place as a guarantee of safety, the prophet Jeremiah said in God's name, “But go now to the place in Shiloh where I first made a dwelling for My Name, and see what I did to it because of the wickedness of My people Israel” (Jeremiah 7:12).

John's Gospel uses the picture of God's tent among his people for the coming of Jesus: “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). The Greek verb there means to pitch a tent.
passages.asks: The land was given, the fighting was over, and seven tribes sat still. Ask what God has already given you that you have not gone out to take up: a calling, a reconciliation, a habit of prayer, a gift you have never used. Joshua's cure was to get up and walk the ground and write down what was there. Ask what the first plain, practical step would be for you.

passages.happening:
The first lot comes up for the tribe of Benjamin. “Their allotted territory lay between the tribes of Judah and Joseph” (verse 11).

The writer traces its borders. On the north it runs from the Jordan up past Jericho into the hills toward Bethel (verses 12-13). On the west it turns south to Kiriath-jearim (verse 14). On the south it follows the edge of Judah, down the Valley of Hinnom below the Jebusite city and out to the mouth of the Jordan at the Salt Sea (verses 15-19). On the east the border is the Jordan (verse 20).

Then come its towns, in two groups. The first includes Jericho and Bethel. The second includes Gibeon, Ramah, Mizpeh, Gibeah, and ‘Jebus (that is, Jerusalem)’ (verses 21-28).
passages.hearers:
Benjamin was the youngest of Jacob's sons, and his tribe was small. The lot gave it a narrow strip of hill country squeezed between the two largest tribes. A reader who compares the chapters will see that Benjamin's northern border is Ephraim's southern border, and its southern border is Judah's northern border walked the other way. The pieces fit together.

Small as it was, the strip held places the first half of the book has made familiar: Jericho, where the wall fell; Bethel, beside Ai; and Gibeon, whose people tricked Israel and were kept alive by an oath. The Gibeonites and their towns now lie inside Benjamin.

It also held towns that would matter greatly later. Gibeah was the home of Saul, Israel's first king. Ramah was the home of Samuel. Mizpeh was a gathering place for all Israel in Samuel's day. The apostle Paul, many centuries on, was proud to be of this tribe.

Jerusalem is listed among Benjamin's towns, under its older name Jebus. It stood right on the line between Benjamin and Judah. The book has already said that Judah could not drive out its people, and Judges says the same of Benjamin. Neither tribe held it until David.

One landmark on the southern border is ‘the Stone of Bohan son of Reuben’. Nothing more is known of it. It is a reminder that these borders were walked from one known object to the next by people who had no other kind of map.
passages.later:
Paul gives his descent in a list of things he once counted as gain: ‘of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin’ (Philippians 3:5).

Moses had spoken of this tribe with special tenderness: “May the beloved of the LORD rest secure in Him; God shields him all day long, and upon His shoulders he rests” (Deuteronomy 33:12).
passages.asks: The smallest tribe received a narrow place between two strong neighbors, and some of the most important places in Israel's story turned out to lie in it. Ask whether you think of your own place as too small or too hemmed in to matter. Ask what God may have set inside it that you have not noticed.
